# Abstract

This gazetteer catalogues WGS84 coordinates, geopolitical affiliations, occupation spans and benchmark population trajectories for 1353 early historic settlements across northern South Asia (2,56M km², encompassing 2.558.835 km²) from 600BC to 345BC. Spanning four geopolitical divisions, the gazetteer encompasses diverse architectural and settlement traditions: monumental brick-revetted riverine metropolises of the Ganga and Yamuna doabs, cyclopean mountain valley fortresses in Magadha, fortified gateway entreposts along the north-western Uttarapatha, and strategic crossroads centres connecting the Gangetic basin with the Malwa plateau and Deccan routes.

Settlement sizes range from agrarian hamlets and fortified market towns to premier imperial metropolises led by Delhi (Indraprastha) at 166,56k peak, Varanasi (Kashi) at 138,8k peak, Patna (Pataliputra) at 125,94k peak, Lahore at 110,65k peak, Multan at 64,77k peak, Ujjain (Ujjayini) at 60,15k peak, Peshawar (Purushapura) at 58,81k peak, Mathura at 46,27k peak, Taxila (Takshashila) at 46,27k peak, Kaushambi at 37,01k peak, Bharuch (Bharukachha) at 36,89k peak, Rajgir (Rajagriha) at 32,39k peak, Shravasti at 32,39k peak, Ayodhya at 32,39k peak, Sialkot (Sagala) at 32,27k peak, Mahasthangarh (Pundranagara) at 31,67k peak, Vaishali at 27,76k peak, Bhagalpur (Champa) at 27,76k peak and Vidisha (Besnagar) at 27,76k peak. Every catalogued settlement reconciles against 1.960 source-ledger candidates under INDUS alongside 800 documented exclusions (predominantly duplicate-alias consolidations within a three-kilometre radius).

By coupling georeferenced settlement trajectories with regional hydro-alluvial catchments, this gazetteer establishes an archaeological baseline for early historic nucleation in South Asia. Settlement subtraction isolates nucleated urban centres from rural populations, ensuring that historical demographic reconstructions reflect genuine archaeological site densities rather than speculative continental assumptions.

# Early Historic Settlement Patterns in Northern South Asia

Archaeological settlement patterns in northern South Asia between 600BC and 345BC reflect complex adaptations to regional riverine hydrology, agrarian carrying capacity and inter-regional commercial corridors [@Dwivedi2019Early; @Hussain2026Geopolitic]. Four primary settlement traditions characterise the regional archaeological record:

1. Fortified Riverine Metropolises: Positioned along the high alluvial bluffs of the Ganga, Yamuna and Ghaghara rivers, major capitals such as Kaushambi, Varanasi, Pataliputra, Champa and Shravasti were enclosed by massive earthen ramparts revetted with baked brick and surrounded by deep water-filled moats fed by seasonal river channels [@Dwivedi2019Early; @Donnelly2012Splendour]. These cities operated as political capitals, major craft manufacturing centres and riverine transhipment ports commanding agricultural hinterlands.
2. Mountain-Encircled Valley Fortresses: Exemplified by Rajagriha (Rajgir) in Magadha, this tradition utilised natural amphitheatre ridges of quartzite hills reinforced by cyclopean stone masonry ramparts extending over forty kilometres [@Donnelly2012Splendour]. The valley floor accommodated the royal citadel, residential quarters and Buddhist monastic retreats such as the Gridhrakuta peak and Venuvana bamboo grove [@Shimada2012Early].
3. Northern Highway Gateway Entreposts: Anchored along the Uttarapatha trade artery in the north-west, settlements such as Takshashila (Taxila), Pushkalavati (Charsadda) and Mathura served as cultural and economic gateways between South Asia and Central Asia [@Mishra2026Historical; @Butt2022Indian]. Residential architecture featured stone and mud-brick dwellings arranged around internal courtyards, supported by ironworking, lapidary industries and monetary banking [@Donnelly2012Splendour; @Pradeep2016Making].
4. Strategic Crossroads Capitals: Situated on the Malwa plateau and southern trade routes, cities such as Ujjayini (Ujjain), Vidisha (Besnagar) and Ahichhatra commanded the interfaces between agrarian river basins and mineral-rich forested uplands [@Sharma2018Mauryan; @Pratap2024Ideas]. These sites acted as manufacturing hubs for carnelian beads, copper smelting and iron tools, channelling northern prestige goods to peninsular markets [@Malapaka2025Archaeocer].

# Methodology and Source Ledger Reconciliation

Candidate sites in the source ledger were evaluated using published excavation reports from the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), state archaeology departments, university monographs and stratigraphic radiocarbon syntheses [@Dwivedi2019Early; @Malapaka2025Archaeocer]. Inclusion requires:
- Precise WGS84 geographic coordinates validated against regional river networks and satellite imagery.
- Documented cultural horizons associated with Painted Grey Ware, Northern Black Polished Ware or Early Historic strata.
- Population series calibrated to urban rampart enclosures, mound extent and domestic house densities.

Where multiple survey points fall within three kilometres of a primary nucleated settlement, secondary coordinates are consolidated as duplicate aliases, preserving geographic integrity and preventing artificial clustering.

# Sub-Regional Settlement Catalogues

## Gandhara, Kamboja and North-Western Uttarapatha

The north-western division catalogues 323 settlements spanning the Kabul, Swat, Indus and upper Punjab river basins [@Witzel2008Developmen; @Butt2022Indian]. Taxila (Takshashila), centred at the Bhir Mound, was the pre-eminent urban nexus, concentrating 46,27k inhabitants at its peak and controlling the gateway between the Indian plains and Central Asian trade networks [@Donnelly2012Splendour].

Pushkalavati (Charsadda), situated at the confluence of the Swat and Kabul rivers, served as the western capital of Gandhara, supporting 27,76k inhabitants behind monumental mud-brick defences [@Donnelly2012Splendour]. Other leading centres include Lahore (110,65k peak), Multan (64,77k peak), Peshawar (Purushapura, 58,81k peak) and Sialkot (Sagala, 32,27k peak), accompanied by protohistoric tell mounds at Akra and Harappa.

## Kuru, Panchala, Surasena and Matsya (Upper Ganga-Yamuna)

The Upper Ganga-Yamuna plain catalogues 363 settlements, representing the densest concentration of early historic tell sites in the doab [@Dwivedi2019Early; @Malapaka2025Archaeocer]. Delhi (Indraprastha) anchored the northern narrows between the Yamuna and Aravalli hills, concentrating 166,56k inhabitants at its urban zenith.

Varanasi (Kashi), positioned at the eastern margin of the doab, supported 138,8k inhabitants at its peak, celebrated for its textile guilds, ivory carving and religious sanctity [@Donnelly2012Splendour]. Mathura on the Yamuna concentrated 46,27k people, acting as the primary junction between the northern Uttarapatha and southern routes to Malwa [@Hussain2026Geopolitic]. Kaushambi, capital of Vatsa, housed 37,01k inhabitants behind massive kiln-fired brick ramparts [@Dwivedi2019Early]. In Panchala, Ahichhatra supported 18,51k people, while Kampilya and Hastinapura formed major political centres [@Malapaka2025Archaeocer].

## Kosala, Malla, Vajji, Kashi, Magadha and Anga (Middle Ganga Core)

The Middle Ganga Core catalogues 105 settlements, characterised by extensive urban metropolises and fortified republican assemblies [@Niraula2026Unmasking; @Dwivedi2021Political]. Patna (Pataliputra), founded as a strategic border fortress by Ajatashatru and expanded by Udayin, peaked at 125,94k inhabitants, emerging as the imperial capital of Magadha [@Donnelly2012Splendour].

Rajgir (Rajagriha), the ancient upland capital of Magadha, supported 32,39k people within its natural amphitheatre of hills and cyclopean stone walls [@Donnelly2012Splendour]. In Kosala, Shravasti and Ayodhya concentrated 32,39k inhabitants each, surrounded by earthen ramparts and moat systems [@Anand2017Awadh]. Vaishali, the capital of the Vajji confederacy, housed 27,76k citizens, governed by its celebrated municipal assembly [@Niraula2026Unmasking; @Long2026Buddhism]. Champa (Bhagalpur), capital of Anga, concentrated 27,76k people as the principal eastern river port commanding trade towards the Bengal delta and Bay of Bengal [@Donnelly2012Splendour].

## Avanti, Chedi, Vatsa and Assaka (Malwa-Deccan Crossroads)

The southern division catalogues 369 settlements across the Malwa plateau, Vindhyan hills and northern Deccan [@Sharma2018Mauryan; @Pratap2024Ideas]. Ujjain (Ujjayini), capital of northern Avanti, was the premier metropolis of the crossroads, supporting 60,15k inhabitants behind an enormous clay rampart revetted with brick [@Malapaka2025Archaeocer].

Bharuch (Bharukachha), situated at the mouth of the Narmada on the Gulf of Khambhat, housed 36,89k inhabitants as the primary maritime outlet for northern commodities [@Hussain2026Geopolitic]. Vidisha (Besnagar) on the Betwa river supported 27,76k people, functioning as a vital trade hub where iron, copper and stone resources were processed [@Sharma2018Mauryan]. In the eastern coastal corridor, Sisupalgarh in Kalinga concentrated 27,66k inhabitants within a square layout enclosed by monumental brick-and-earth ramparts [@Smith2016Finding].

# Source Ledger Audit and Excluded Candidates

The INDUS source ledger records 1.960 candidates for the Mahajanapada era. Of these, 1.160 were included as primary catalogued settlements with chronological population series, while 800 entries were excluded.

All 800 exclusions represent duplicate-alias consolidations: satellite survey coordinates or secondary archaeological findspots located within a three-kilometre radius of a primary nucleated settlement that were merged into the canonical site to avoid artificial spatial over-concentration.

Table \ref{tab:excluded} documents the leading 25 excluded candidates alongside their canonical primary settlement and justification.

# Limitations and Preservation Biases

Archaeological visibility across early historic northern South Asia remains shaped by differential taphonomy and modern development:
1. Continuous Urban Overbuilding: Major ancient metropolises such as Varanasi, Delhi, Patna, Mathura and Ujjain remain densely populated modern urban centres, constraining excavations to rescue trenches in public parks or peripheral mounds [@Donnelly2012Splendour].
2. Fluvial Channel Migration and Silting: The dynamic meandering of the Ganga, Yamuna and Indus rivers has eroded ancient riverfront wharves and buried early historic cultural levels beneath deep alluvial silts [@Mishra2026Historical].
3. Perishable Building Traditions: While monumental ramparts utilised burnt brick and cyclopean stone, domestic structures were predominantly erected with sundried mud-brick, timber frames and thatched roofs, leaving ephemeral posthole sequences in monsoonal soils.

Despite these taphonomic factors, the integration of 1.160 catalogued settlements establishes an empirical foundation for early historic urban demography in South Asia.
